extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, curriculum designers, and administrators responsible for quantitative literacy/general education programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and program-level standards for designing, operating, and assessing undergraduate quantitative literacy requirements and courses (examples from Macalester, Juniata, and Dominican). Focuses on curriculum options, course design, faculty support, assessment, outreach, and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique graduation requirement (QM4PP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are not able to satisfy this requirement with any other course in mathematics or any other quantitative subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intention is to make enrollment in at least one participating QM4PP class a graduation requirement that cannot be satisfied by other courses; timeline noted (target by summer 2006). Purpose is to ensure centrality of the program to the college’s quantitative-literacy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty engagement and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage and support participation by faculty who normally would not teach courses with a quantitative component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design includes stipends, workshops, and support personnel to lower barriers; messaging should avoid conveying that quantitative methods are the only foundation for policy decisions to retain goodwill among math-averse faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual and planning workshops around a policy topic
rubrics_metrics.description: An annual workshop built around the policy topic for the following year designed to acquaint a broad range of faculty with how quantitative methods come into play in thinking about this issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a two-day preliminary January workshop to evaluate and plan and a three-day primary summer workshop to learn policy questions, identify quantitative emphases, bring in speakers (local and nationally recognized), and sketch semester topics. First-time participating faculty receive a summer stipend ($2500 in this example). Workshops can include outreach to faculty from other institutions and secondary teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicated support personnel for program implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide staff/faculty whose role is to help quantitatively literate faculty tie their courses to the policy topic and to help non-quantitative faculty bring quantitative ideas into their syllabi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example staffing: one faculty member released from one course annually plus a Policy Associate who teaches one participating class and spends remaining time supporting other faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student placement and enrollment policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Students in multi-section courses may choose to enroll in a participating or non-participating section; long-term goal is mandatory enrollment in at least one participating class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During pilot phases allow choice; plan transition to requirement once program reputation is established; ensure the requirement cannot be satisfied by other courses to emphasize program distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common evening class requirement and format
rubrics_metrics.description: All students in participating classes must register for a common evening class (Wednesday evenings), which carries 1 credit and is graded pass/fail; prior attendees may be exempt from registration though instructors may require attendance on specific evenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evening class structure: roughly half topics quantitative and half policy; large scale presentations (up to 200–300 students) followed by small-group activities; one faculty member coordinates but many presenters lead sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evening class small-group pedagogy and semester project
rubrics_metrics.description: After presentations, students break into groups of ~6 (mixed across classes) to work on activities and consolidate understanding; groups complete a semester-long project (e.g., in-depth critique of a controversial paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty from participating classes and trained undergraduate preceptors circulate to assist; group composition promotes interdisciplinary interaction and individualized help; projects emphasize critique of quantitative components of articles/opinion pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre/post assessment using article critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary assessment focused on students’ ability to critique statements made by others: give students newspaper articles at semester start and again at the end and ask them to critique selected items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginning-of-semester random article assignment; end-of-semester exam includes same articles among a larger set; students critique two articles. This measures improvement in critical quantitative evaluation skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-method assessment strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine quantitative and qualitative assessment: professional consultant, on-campus assessment coordinator, focus groups, individual interviews, and a longitudinal study of selected students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mixed methods to gather perceptions of learning, value of experience, and improvements; longitudinal interviews can track development across semesters and contribute to accreditation evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-disciplinary departmental commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Build program foundations across multiple departments (mathematics, economics, geography, political science, communication, English, etc.) with departmental chairs’ support to ensure participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize obstacles (departmental reluctance to require evening component while program is unproven) and emphasize cooperation; include departments outside mathematics to teach quantitative material in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outreach, dissemination, and materials sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of funding mandates, programs should provide outreach and dissemination: host faculty from other institutions, provide materials (slides, worksheets), and offer small adaptation subgrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Website resources (PowerPoints, worksheets), funding to underwrite workshop attendance for external faculty, and subgrants to support local adaptation and potential NSF proposals for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple acceptable routes to satisfy a campus quantitative requirement (Juniata model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must demonstrate basic competence in statistics and basic mathematical skills; satisfy via (1) completion of a combined 'Q' course, (2) completion of separate statistical (QS) and mathematical (QM) courses, or (3) pass proficiency exams in math and statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides flexibility to fit students’ majors and backgrounds; tracks how students satisfy the requirement and recognizes variation in skills acquired through different routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core statistical competencies for QS courses
rubrics_metrics.description: QS competency set includes sampling, data organization and representation, measures of central tendency, measures of dispersion, and elementary probability concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QS courses may be offered across departments (e.g., chemistry-biology labs, biostatistics, social sciences statistics) and should include applied data collection, use of technology where appropriate, and written interpretation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core mathematical/problem-solving competencies for QM courses
rubrics_metrics.description: QM courses should provide understanding of percentages, ratios, proportionality, rates of change, linear functions and two-variable linear systems, emphasizing combined algebraic, graphical, and numerical approaches and word-problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of reform calculus and Rule of 3 (expanded to Rule of 4 including writing) encouraged; present algebraic, graphical, numerical algorithms and document approaches; courses can be distributed across relevant departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-world word problems and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Course problems should be word problems using real-world data wherever feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Quantitative Methods text updates real data yearly (federal budget, salaries, populations); word-problem focus aligns course work with applications students will face outside academia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-solution pedagogy (Rule of 3/4)
rubrics_metrics.description: When feasible, present problems solved algebraically, graphically, and numerically (Rule of 3), and include writing to learn as a fourth approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how different approaches relate and lead to the same result; example: finding maxima/minima via plotting/zooming, numerical checking, and algebraic manipulation; emphasize documenting reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and documentation requirements in quantitative courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must document their reasoning and explain conclusions; major projects are written as articles with embedded equations, tables, and graphs (MS Word).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two major course projects (end of statistics and mathematics sections) require polished written presentation; routine homework and computer assignments also require written interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic thinking and integration of programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the concept of 'algorithm' as a fundamental conceptual tool and teach short programs/macros to implement algorithms (e.g., Minitab macros, Maple procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algorithmic development to illuminate formulas (e.g., standard deviation in frequency distributions), to automate repetitive numerical tasks, and to enable students to derive algebraic formulas by following algorithmic procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology integration with math/stat focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate technology (statistics packages, calculators, computer algebra systems) while keeping the emphasis on mathematics/statistics rather than on the computer itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Juniata, statistics implemented in Minitab and mathematics/programming in Maple; technology supports problem solving (e.g., computer demos in lab), but instruction stresses understanding over tool-centered training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based learning and collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: All work (including exams) in some courses is done in teams of two to foster interaction and reduce student stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair/team assignments encourage peer learning and can make math classes less intimidating for math-averse students; instructors should design tasks to promote constructive collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course structure and assignment patterns (Quantitative Methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative Methods is a three-credit course meeting three one-hour lectures plus a one-hour lab/help session; homework assigned daily with weekly computer assignments and midterm/final projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lab classroom with PCs allows students to work along; computer demonstrations and Maple/Minitab assignments support multiple-solution pedagogy; deliverables include Word projects with embedded artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-level assessment benchmarks and evidence (use of standardized tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use external standardized measures where appropriate (e.g., PPST:M categories) and report pass rates as part of assessment evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Education majors required to pass the PPST:M; Juniata reports a 99% pass rate for their cohort. Use such evidence as one part of a mixed-methods assessment portfolio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance that different pathways produce varied skill profiles but shared 'habit of mind'
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple routes to the quantitative requirement mean not every student will have identical skills, but the aim is a shared habit of mind: applying statistics and mathematics in context (skills listed by the Design Team: arithmetic, data, computers, modeling, statistics, chance, reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design should emphasize common cognitive approaches and dispositions even if specific technical competencies differ; document curricular paths and expected learning outcomes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit departmental examples linking content to quantitative literacy outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Course examples showing how specific courses satisfy QS/QM competencies (e.g., chemistry labs use 95% CI and t-tests; statistics for social sciences emphasizes conditions for tests and interpretation; managerial accounting emphasizes spreadsheets and non-technical memos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide syllabi-level evidence and sample assignments that map course activities to stated competencies; require written interpretation/communication components to demonstrate applied understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear learning goals for revised mathematics requirements (Dominican University)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to: understand and use numbers and mathematical symbols; think logically to solve problems; manipulate and understand algebraic expressions; model real life problems using mathematics; read and understand mathematical information in the media and professional literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These goals may be demonstrated via placement examination or by completing specified college-level coursework (College Algebra, Mathematics for Elementary Teachers, Finite Mathematics, Contemporary Mathematics); optional graphing-calculator components recognized but not uniformly required.
